sections.h2: Which Elyria office files a Lorain County deed?
sections.html:
Deeds, mortgages and land contracts for Lorain County go to the Recorder at 226 Middle Avenue, Room 102, Elyria, OH 44035. The office answers at 440-329-5148 and lists weekday hours of 8 AM to 4 PM on its home page.

The Recorder keeps the land record and nothing else. Its FAQ page says the office does not hand out blank forms, fill in forms, alter a deed, settle ownership disputes, or search for liens on your behalf. For those jobs, hire a title company or attorney. The same page says the county's land records reach back to 1824 and that a free copy of your own deed can be pulled from the online property search, with certified copies available at the counter.

sections.h2: What is the Lorain County Recorder's fee for a deed?
sections.html:
The 2026 fee page prints $39.00 for the first two pages of a deed, mortgage, lease or affidavit, plus $8.00 for each page after that. Each printed side counts as a page, so a deed printed front and back on two sheets is four pages.

Standard charges on the Lorain County Recorder's 2026 fee page
ItemCharge printed
Deed, mortgage, lease, affidavit, first two pages$39.00
Each page after the second$8.00
Marginal notation (release, assignment, amendment)$4.00 each, added to the recording fee
Regular copy$2.00 per page
Certified copy$2.00 per page plus $1.00 for the seal
Real estate financing statement$12.00 plus $4.00 per name indexed
Federal tax lien$5.00, release $3.00
Document that breaks the layout rules$20.00 extra

The page explains that state law splits the fee in half. One half is the basic recording fee and the other half goes to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. A notice on the same page, dated 01/01/2026, adds that a $5.00 preservation surcharge raised the standard fee to its current level. The page also shows a sample chart: three pages cost $47.00, five pages cost $63.00, and ten pages cost $103.00.

sections.h2: What must happen at the Lorain County Auditor before the Recorder will take a deed?
sections.html:
The deed has to be endorsed by the Auditor first. Under section 319.202, the buyer files a statement of the property's value, and the Auditor writes the conveyance fee on the face of the deed. The seller pays that fee.

The Lorain County Auditor's transfer page sets practical limits that catch people out:

  • Transfers run Monday through Thursday, 8 AM to 4 PM. Friday is not a transfer day.
  • E-filed transfers stop at 3 PM. In-person transfers stop at 4 PM.
  • Mail is refused. Since November 1, 2012, real estate transfers must come in person or through an approved e-file vendor.
  • Handwritten forms are refused. Forms must be typed and complete, with the right conveyance or exempt form attached.
  • Incomplete packets or wrong fees are returned, and the office does not hold them for later.

The Auditor's staff may not complete the forms or advise on them, citing section 4705.01 of the Revised Code. Ask the closing agent or your attorney to prepare the packet.

sections.h2: How is the conveyance fee set, and which deeds are exempt?
sections.html:
Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the statewide piece at one dollar, or ten cents for each $100 of value, whichever is greater. A county may add its own transfer tax of up to thirty cents per $100 under section 322.02. Ask the Auditor which rate applies in Lorain County before you budget for closing.

The statute lists many transfers that owe no conveyance fee. The seller still writes the reason for the exemption on the form. Ones that come up in family and estate sales:

  • A gift between spouses, or between a parent and child.
  • A deed that corrects or confirms an earlier recorded deed.
  • A deed given only to secure or release a debt.
  • A transfer among heirs or devisees of one decedent when no money changes hands.
  • A transfer into, or out of, a revocable trust.
  • A transfer where the value is $100 or less.

A separate charge applies to every transfer: fifty cents for each parcel entered, paid by the person asking for the transfer.

sections.h2: What layout mistakes add $20 to a Lorain County recording?
sections.html:
Any document prepared after June 30, 2009 must follow the standardization rules in section 317.114, and the Recorder collects $20.00 more when it does not. The rules on the Lorain County fee page are:

  • Type of at least 10 point on paper from 8.5 by 11 to 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Black or blue ink only, with no highlighting.
  • One inch of margin at each side and at the bottom.
  • A three inch blank band at the top of page one, reserved for the recorder, auditor and engineer.
  • A one and a half inch top margin on each later page.

Court papers, tax authority papers, plats, DD-214 discharges, state and federal documents, and anything signed before the law took effect are exempt. The Recorder offers a downloadable template on its fee page.

sections.h2: What is Lorain County like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Lorain County sits on Lake Erie in northeast Ohio, west of Cuyahoga County. Its 923 square miles include 432 of water, which is 47 percent of the total, according to Wikipedia's county entry citing Census figures. Elyria holds the courthouse, while the city of Lorain has the most residents. The county's cities are Amherst, Avon, Avon Lake, Elyria, Lorain, North Ridgeville, Oberlin, Sheffield Lake and Vermilion.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for Lorain County shows 323,219 residents in July 2025 and 139,777 housing units. The 2020 to 2024 survey figures are a median owner-occupied home value of $223,200, median household income of $73,347, and an owner-occupancy rate of 74.0 percent. Median gross rent was $966. Those numbers describe a county where most households own, so most sellers will be recording a deed they received through an earlier purchase or an estate.

sections.h2: How can a Lorain County owner watch for deed fraud?
sections.html:
The Recorder offers a free property alert sign-up on its website. Its FAQ describes deed fraud as someone transferring a property without the owner's knowledge, and suggests owners monitor their records, treat unsolicited deed offers with caution, and sign up for alerts.

The same advice helps anyone selling an inherited or tenant-occupied house. Search your own parcel in the online property search before you list it, confirm that the name on the last recorded deed matches the person signing, and keep a certified copy for the closing file. If the record shows a mortgage or lien that was paid off long ago, the release still has to be recorded, at the $4.00 marginal notation charge printed on the fee page.

sections.h2: How has Lorain County grown, and why does page count matter?
sections.html:
Lorain County grew in waves. Wikipedia shows a population of 5,696 in 1830, a jump to 217,500 by 1960, and 312,964 in 2020. The county was physically set up in 1822 and became judicially independent in 1824, and Oberlin College is based there.

Page count drives the recording bill, so ask whoever prepares your deed to keep the document short. On the Recorder's own sample chart, each added page costs the same $8.00, so a long exhibit adds up. If the deed carries a reference to an older document, expect the $4.00 marginal notation charge on top.

sections.h2: What do I bring on closing day for a Lorain County transfer?
sections.html:
A short checklist keeps the Auditor and the Recorder from sending the packet back:

  • The signed and notarized deed, typed, with the legal description and parcel numbers.
  • The correct conveyance form, or the exempt form with the reason written out.
  • Payment of the conveyance fee and the fifty cents per parcel to the Auditor.
  • A check for the Recorder's page-count fee, using the sample chart as a guide.
  • A self-check that every page is typed in black or blue ink, with the margins the layout rules call for.

Because the Auditor handles transfers only Monday through Thursday and cuts off e-files at 3 PM, a Friday closing needs the deed endorsed earlier in the week or submitted by a vendor on Thursday.

faqs.q: What will Lorain County charge me at the counter for a deed?
faqs.a: The 2026 fee page prints $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for every page after that. Add $4.00 for each marginal notation, such as a mortgage release, and $20.00 if the layout breaks the state standardization rules. The conveyance fee at the Auditor is separate.

faqs.q: Can I mail a deed to the Lorain County Auditor?
faqs.a: No. The Auditor stopped accepting real estate transfers by U.S. mail on November 1, 2012. Bring the deed in person Monday through Thursday, or use an approved e-file vendor, which must submit by 3 PM.

faqs.q: Does the Lorain County Recorder search for liens or fix a deed?
faqs.a: No. The Recorder says it is not trained to search for liens on your behalf and cannot alter a deed. A title company or attorney handles lien searches and corrective deeds.

faqs.q: Which office handles Lorain County property taxes?
faqs.a: The County Treasurer and County Auditor, not the Recorder. The Recorder's FAQ states plainly that property taxes sit with those two offices. Ask them for current-year amounts before closing.

faqs.q: How far back do Lorain County land records go?
faqs.a: The Recorder's FAQ says property records date to 1824, kept in both paper archives and digital form. The online property search lets you view and download a free copy of a recorded deed.
